extracted.intended_audience: editors and readers interested in textual variants / literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing a new edition of an old poem: how to present variant readings from earlier editions and manuscripts and how to choose among conflicting readings (metre, rhyme, sense, manuscript authority, paleographic errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present various readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an old Ode to the Publick in a new Edition, with the several various Readings which I find of it in former Editions, and in Ancient Manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print and record the alternative readings found across earlier editions and ancient manuscripts so readers can see textual variation; include the principal song or poem itself for readers who do not relish the apparatus of variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve metre; restore genuine reading by observing synæresis
rubrics_metrics.description: If an editorial reading (e.g., Aldus's 'ever') would hurt the Metre, restore it to its genuine Reading by observing that Synæresis which had been neglected by ignorant Transcribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metrical considerations to prefer readings that fit the poem's established metre; correct negligent transcriptions by applying legitimate metrical/phonological operations (like synæresis) rather than accepting variants that disrupt metre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and respect original orthography where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'and' in some Manuscripts is written thus, '&', but that in the Cotton Library writes it in three distinct Letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note orthographic differences (contractions, ampersands, spellings) in manuscripts rather than silently modernizing them; preserve or report distinctive letter-forms where they may affect reading or textual history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and correct paleographic/scribal errors by close examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vatican Manuscript for 'I' reads 'it', but this must have been the Hallucination of the Transcriber, who probably mistook the Dash of the I for a T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to plausible scribal mistakes (misread letters, miscopied strokes/dashes) and correct them when paleographic evidence supports correction; avoid adopting obvious hallucinations of transcribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the usual/established reading absent strong contrary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Scioppius, Salmasius and many others, for 'the' read 'a', but I have stuck to the usual Reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with competing readings, default to the established/common reading unless manuscript authority or internal criteria (metre, sense, external evidence) provide a compelling reason to alter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contextual and external evidence to choose grammatical/gender readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Manuscripts have it 'his' Wit, others 'your', others 'their' Wit. But as I find Corinna to be the Name of a Woman in other Authors, I cannot doubt but it should be 'her'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between variant pronouns or gendered forms by using contextual clues and concordances in other authors; prefer readings consistent with known names or usages unless manuscripts strongly contradict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve rhyme and sense when selecting variants
rubrics_metrics.description: The German Manuscript reads a lasting 'Passion', but the Rhyme will not admit it. ... First, because the Rhime, and, Secondly, because the Sense is preserved by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to rhyme and semantic coherence in verse-editing: prefer readings that maintain the poem's rhyme-scheme and overall sense; reject otherwise attractive emendations that create defective rhyme or distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid emending proper names without strong manuscript support; consider but do not impose etymology
rubrics_metrics.description: Did not all the Manuscripts reclaim, I should change Belvidera into Pelvidera; Pelvis being used by several of the Ancient Comick Writers for a Looking-glass, by which means the Etymology of the Word is very visible, and Pelvidera will signifie a Lady who often looks in her Glass; ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although etymological reasoning can suggest emendations (e.g., a name's derivation), do not change established proper names unless the manuscript evidence decisively supports the emendation; speculative etymological corrections should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh unanimous manuscript readings against possible cipher/scribal errors; defer when uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the Ancient Manuscripts have it 'in two'. Indeed so many of them concur in this last reading, that I am very much in doubt whether it ought not to take place. ... they perhaps mistook the Dash for a second Figure, and by casting up both together composed out of them the Figure 2. But this I shall leave to the Learned, without determining any thing in a Matter of so great Uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when many manuscripts agree on a reading, consider whether a common scribal practice (such as writing numbers in cypher or misreading a pen-stroke) could have produced the unanimity; if uncertainty remains, acknowledge the doubt and defer decisive emendation to specialist judgment rather than forcing an uncertain change.
